Fifth CircuitPublished opinionSep 30, 2026

Domanic v. Christian Brothers Automotive Corporation

U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit · 25-20486

The court affirmed summary judgment for a Christian franchisor on a Jewish applicant’s § 1981 claim. It distinguished religious discrimination from ancestry-based discrimination and found no evidence that the Christian-only franchise policy masked racial discrimination. The majority did not decide the asserted ministerial-exception defense.

Young v. NHE Inc.

U.S. District Court, Northern District of Mississippi · 4:25-cv-201-DMB-DAS · Doc. 12

The court dismissed a former employee’s religious-discrimination and religious-speech claims. The Title VII claim was untimely, and the complaint did not allege facts making the private employer a governmental actor subject to First Amendment restrictions. The dismissal rested on those legal barriers rather than a trial determination of the discrimination allegations.

State courtDiscovery mandamusAug 31, 2026

In re Institute in Basic Life Principles, Inc.

Texas Sixth Court of Appeals, Texarkana · 06-26-00079-CV

The court conditionally granted mandamus directing the trial court to vacate an overbroad discovery order in a civil abuse-related lawsuit. It resolved the dispute under procedural discovery rules rather than deciding IBLP’s constitutional objection. It also instructed further proceedings to respect earlier guidance against inquiries into protected religious doctrine.

Procedural context: The constitutional question was not decided. This was not a blanket religious privilege or immunity from suit.

In re Gateway Church, Willbanks, Fambro, and Minor

Texas Fifth Court of Appeals, Dallas · 05-25-01527-CV

The court held that defamation-related claims against Gateway Church and three elders were inseparable from the church’s investigation and communications concerning its pastor. State courtMixed summary judgment orderJul 15, 2026

Jeremiah Counsel Corporation v. Young

Texas Business Court, Eleventh Division · 25-BC11B-0031 · 2026 Tex. Bus. 46

In a dispute over Second Baptist Church of Houston’s governance, the court barred claims requiring it to evaluate religious descriptions or second-guess ecclesiastical decisions. It separately applied neutral corporate-law principles, invalidating a 2023 amendment to the church’s articles while rejecting the challenge to its bylaws. The mixed ruling illustrates the boundary between protected church autonomy and enforceable secular corporate requirements.

Procedural context: An accounting claim remained; the order did not dismiss the entire lawsuit.

State courtSummary judgment orderJul 14, 2026

Sri Shirdi Sai Baba Temple of Austin v. Lam

Texas Business Court, Third Division · 25-BC03A-0020 · 2026 Tex. Bus. 45

The court held that neutral Texas corporate law could resolve a temple’s governance dispute without deciding religious questions. Its certificate of formation controlled over conflicting bylaws that purported to shift management from directors to members. The court granted defendants’ summary-judgment motion and denied plaintiffs’ motion, while leaving attorney’s fees for later determination.

Procedural context: Attorney’s fees remained pending; this was not a final judgment.

Young v. Town of Coffeeville

U.S. District Court, Northern District of Mississippi · 3:25-cv-49-DAS · Doc. 108

The court rejected an unpaid municipal intern’s claims arising from restrictions on unsolicited religious discussions with town-hall visitors. Any Title VII theory had been abandoned and also failed because the internship was unpaid.

Fifth CircuitPublished opinionJun 25, 2026

Davis v. Guerrero

U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit · 24-70008

The court affirmed denial of habeas relief to a Texas death-row prisoner who challenged the use of his Satanist affiliation and materials at sentencing. Applying AEDPA’s deferential standard, it held that the state court’s rejection of his First Amendment claim did not conflict unreasonably with clearly established Supreme Court law.

Procedural context: This is a deferential federal habeas decision, not a general authorization to punish religious belief.

Federal districtMotion to dismiss deniedJun 24, 2026

East Plano Islamic Center v. Texas Funeral Services Commission

U.S. District Court, Western District of Texas · 1:25-cv-01085-DAE · Doc. 58

The court allowed EPIC’s individual-capacity claims against former commission presiding officer Kristin Tips to proceed. It held that allegations of religiously discriminatory enforcement against Islamic funeral rites sufficiently pleaded violations of clearly established Free Exercise and Equal Protection rights. This denied Tips’s motion to dismiss; it was not a final finding that all allegations were proved.

Procedural context: This order addressed Tips’s motion. It reserved the commission defendants’ separate motion.

U.S. Supreme CourtMerits opinionJun 23, 2026

Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

U.S. Supreme Court · 23-1197 · 609 U.S. 59

The Court affirmed dismissal of a Rastafarian prisoner’s RLUIPA damages claims against Louisiana corrections officers who allegedly forcibly shaved his head. Because the officers had not knowingly and voluntarily agreed to personal liability under the statute’s federal-funding conditions, the Spending Clause did not permit those claims. The Court did not decide whether RLUIPA otherwise authorizes money damages.

U.S. Supreme CourtMerits opinionJun 23, 2026

Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe

U.S. Supreme Court · 24-856 · 609 U.S. 141

Falun Gong practitioners alleged that Cisco supplied surveillance technology enabling religious persecution in China. The Court reversed and remanded, holding that federal courts cannot create new causes of action under the Alien Tort Statute for violations of international norms and that the Torture Victim Protection Act does not authorize aiding-and-abetting liability.

Procedural context: A civil-remedies decision involving religious-persecution allegations, rather than a domestic Free Exercise holding.

Leach v. Gateway Church

U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Texas · 4:24-cv-00885-ALM · Doc. 101

The court dismissed congregants’ claims challenging Gateway Church’s allocation of donated tithes. Applying Fifth Circuit church-autonomy precedent, it concluded that deciding whether spending fulfilled the church’s religious mission would require an impermissible inquiry into ecclesiastical matters. The ruling closed the civil action; it did not adjudicate whether the alleged financial misconduct occurred.

How the court watch works

The initial look-back covers May 15 through November 11, 2026. The displayed collection then rolls forward over 180 days. The case blurbs were checked against court opinions, filed orders, and official dockets; each entry identifies its source and review date. Summaries distinguish allegations from findings, merits decisions from procedural rulings, and later stays where verified.

Daily checks search CourtListener’s public opinion feeds for religious liberty, free exercise, church autonomy, religious discrimination and accommodation, RFRA, RLUIPA, the Establishment Clause, and the ministerial exception. New matches appear automatically under “Opinion matches,” with attributed excerpts. Keyword matches can be incidental; they are not promoted automatically into source-checked holdings or attributed to Eric Hudson as reviewed analysis.

Coverage includes the U.S. Supreme Court, the Fifth Circuit, federal district courts in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, and indexed state-court opinions in those three states. Public feed coverage is uneven, especially for trial-court and emergency orders. The initial research found no source-checked Louisiana state or federal district entry for this window; that is a coverage gap, not a conclusion that none exists. This service is not a complete docket search, citator, or automatic appeal-status check. A daily feed check does not reverify every older case’s current validity.
